transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess the biggest thing is I’m not really eating right anymore. Like, I’ll go most of the day and it’s just coffee, maybe a piece of bread if I can make myself grab something. It’s not like I’m trying to diet or anything, it just… food doesn’t really happen. And now my pants are getting loose, like hanging on me, and that kind of scared me when I noticed it. I figured I should probably talk to somebody because it’s gotten pretty bad.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah… yeah, I have. Most days it’s like I wake up and before I even really think about anything, there’s this heavy feeling there. Like right in my chest, kind of empty and weighed down at the same time, if that makes sense. It’s not even always that I’m crying or anything dramatic, it’s more like… I open my eyes and it already feels like nothing good is waiting for me. Like the day is just something I have to get through.

I find myself wanting to keep my head down, not really look too far ahead, not think too much. It’s just this low, dark kind of feeling sitting on me most of the time.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… a lot, actually. I used to like doing these little things that weren’t anything big, but they felt like mine, you know? Like I’d go walk by the lake, just kind of clear my head and watch the water, take my time out there. I used to really enjoy that.

And I had these little model kits I’d work on at home. Nothing fancy, just sitting there with the pieces, putting things together bit by bit. It used to feel calming, like I could get absorbed in it.

Now… they just sit there. The boxes and pieces are still there, and I’ll look at them, but it’s like they belong to somebody else. I don’t feel that pull to pick them up. Even walking by the lake sounds like something I should want to do, but I don’t really feel anything about it. It’s like the enjoyment part got switched off somehow.
Have you been having thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

I… I’m not really sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean, I hear what you’re asking, and I don’t want to say the wrong thing and make it sound bigger or smaller than it is.

I guess… I’ve had moments where I feel really worn out by everything, like I don’t want to deal with the day, but when you say “life isn’t worth living” or “hurting myself,” I don’t know if I’d put it that way. I haven’t really sat down and thought it through like that, if that makes sense. It’s more like this tired, empty feeling, and I just kind of go quiet with it.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed myself making any kind of plan or anything like that. I just know I’ve been feeling really low, and it’s been hard to care about much.
Are you avoiding food because you’re worried about gaining weight?

No… no, it’s not really like that. I’m not avoiding food because I’m scared of gaining weight or anything. I don’t think about it that way.

It’s more like… I just hardly eat right anymore. Food doesn’t really pull me in. Some days I’ll get through most of the day on coffee, and then maybe I’ll have a piece of bread or something small, just because it’s there or because I realize I haven’t had anything. It’s not me trying to lose weight.

I’ve noticed my pants are hanging loose on me now, like I have to keep pulling them up, and that kind of made me realize I’m not eating much. But it’s not about wanting to be thinner. It’s just… eating feels like another thing I don’t really have much drive to do.
Did all of this start after a particular stressful event or major change in your life?

Yeah… I think it did kind of start after something big. I got fired, and after that everything sort of… swung really hard. At first it wasn’t just sadness right away, it was like I got this scary kind of driven feeling, like I had to do something, had to prove something, had to keep moving. It felt intense, not normal for me.

And then after that, I dropped down into this low place. That whole swing — from getting fired, to feeling all pushed and wound up, and then ending up like this — has been going on about a month now. It feels longer when I’m in it, honestly, but if I count it out, yeah… around a month.
During that driven period after you got fired, were you needing much less sleep than usual?

Yeah… yeah, I was. That part was really strange, because normally if I only sleep a little, I feel awful the next day. But during that period, I’d sleep maybe two or three hours, sometimes barely that, and then I’d just kind of pop up like I’d had a full night’s rest.

It wasn’t even like I was dragging myself out of bed. I’d wake up and feel like, “Okay, I’m up, I’ve got things to do,” like my body didn’t understand it was supposed to be tired. I remember looking at the time and thinking it was ridiculous, because it would still be dark out, and I should’ve been exhausted, but I wasn’t. I was just… going.
During that driven period, did you also feel unusually euphoric or unusually confident?

Yeah… I did. I mean, “euphoric” sounds a little strong, but I guess there were times it was like that. Right after I got fired, instead of just feeling crushed, I got this feeling like… fine, I’ll show them. Like I was fired up, almost untouchable. Like nobody could really stop me or tell me what to do.

It wasn’t just confidence like a normal good mood, though. It felt bigger than that, like I was suddenly sure I had everything figured out. And if anyone tried to bring me down or say, “Maybe slow down,” or “Think this through,” I’d get irritated really fast. I’d snap at them before they even finished talking, because in my head they were just getting in the way.

So yeah, there was that kind of high, charged-up confidence… but it had an angry edge to it too.
During that charged-up period, were you doing a lot more activities or projects than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I was doing way more than I normally do. It was like I couldn’t sit still at all, like if I sat down for even a minute my body would start buzzing and I’d think, no, I need to get up, I need to do something.

I kept going out and cleaning my tools, even stuff that didn’t really need cleaning. I’d line things up, wipe them down, move them, then come back and mess with them again like there was some important reason for it. And I was moving boxes around too — not even always to a better place, just shifting things, sorting, re-sorting, deciding I had a new plan, then changing it again.

And I kept planning jobs in my head, like all these things I was going to do, ways to make money or fix things or get back on track. It felt like I had a motor running inside me. Not just being productive, more like I couldn’t turn it off.
During that charged-up period, were you talking a lot more than usual?

Yeah… I guess I was. I didn’t really notice it at first, because in my head it felt like I was just explaining what needed to happen, you know? Like I had all these thoughts lined up and I had to get them out before I lost them.

But my sister pointed it out. She said I was talking so fast she could barely get a word in. I was going on and on about prices, and making flyers, and what to say to tenants, and how much things should cost, and how I was going to handle everything. I remember her trying to ask me something, and I’d just keep talking over her, not even meaning to be rude exactly, but I couldn’t stop long enough to let her catch up.

It was like my mouth was trying to keep up with my head, and there was too much coming at once.
During that charged-up period, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive for you?

I’m not really sure how to answer that one. I mean, “risky” can mean different things, right? Like, if you mean did I go out and do something crazy dangerous on purpose, I don’t know that I’d say it that way.

During that time I was definitely acting faster than I normally would, like making decisions before really thinking them through all the way. But when you ask if it was unusually risky or impulsive, I kind of have to stop and think, because in the moment it didn’t feel risky to me. It felt like I was just doing what needed to be done, like I was finally moving instead of sitting around.

Other people might’ve seen it as me being impulsive, I guess, because I wasn’t exactly pausing and weighing things out. But I don’t have one clear thing in my head where I can say, yes, that was definitely some big risky thing. It was more like everything felt urgent, and I’d just jump into stuff without the usual hesitation.
About how many days in a row did that charged-up period last?

It’s kind of hard to pin down exactly to the day, because it didn’t feel like it started and stopped clean, like flipping a switch. But if I’m being honest, that whole scary swing — from when I got fired and then started feeling all driven and wound up, to now being this low — it’s been about a month altogether.

The charged-up part was in there first, after I got fired, and then it… shifted. But the whole thing, the whole run of it where I haven’t felt like myself, has been around a month.
Did that charged-up period last at least 4 days in a row?

I’m not completely sure how to separate it out day by day. It wasn’t like I woke up one morning and could say, okay, this is day one, and then it ended cleanly.

What I can say is that the whole scary swing — from after I got fired, when I started feeling really driven and wound up, to where I am now feeling low — has been going on for about a month. The charged-up part was at the beginning of that. I just don’t know exactly how many days to count for that piece by itself.
During that charged-up period, did it cause serious problems in your life or lead to you being hospitalized?

I didn’t go to the hospital, no. But serious problems… yeah, I mean, it’s been serious in the sense that I’m not functioning like I normally would.

Since it got bad, I’ve had to lean on my relatives for stuff I used to handle myself. Like money things, getting rides places, dealing with paperwork — forms and calls and things like that. I’ll look at something basic that needs to be done and it just doesn’t get done, or I need somebody to sit with me or take me there or remind me what I’m supposed to do.

And errands too. I’m not keeping up with regular errands the way I used to. It’s embarrassing to say, because I’m grown and I don’t like needing that much help, but right now I kind of do. So not hospitalized, but it has definitely messed up my life and made me depend on family more than usual.
During that charged-up period, did your thoughts feel like they were racing?

Yes. That was actually one of the things that scared me, because it wasn’t just like normal thinking or being busy in my head. It felt like my head was packed full of ideas all at once, like one thing would pop up and before I even finished thinking about it, it turned into another plan, and then that would turn into something else.

Like I’d think about one job, or getting work, or fixing one problem, and then suddenly I’d be making this whole other plan in my mind, and then another one after that. It just kept going. I’d try to slow it down, like tell myself, “Okay, just focus on one thing,” but I couldn’t really hold it still. My thoughts kept jumping ahead of me.
During that charged-up period, were you more goal-directed than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, way more than normal for me. I wasn’t just thinking, “I should find some work,” I was kind of acting like I had to build this whole thing right then.

I started calling old tenants I knew, people from before, asking if they needed repairs or knew anybody who did. Then I was making lists — like long lists — of what I could fix, what tools I’d need, what I already had, what I’d have to buy. I was pricing tools, looking at costs, trying to figure out how to line up handyman work, and I’d be doing that all day.

It felt like I couldn’t just leave it alone. Normally I might make one phone call or write down a couple things and then come back to it later, but during that time I was pushing and pushing, like every minute had to be used to get something started. It was a lot more than I’d ever done before.
During that charged-up period, did you feel more powerful, special, or capable than usual?

Yeah… yeah, I did. At the time it didn’t feel like I was being unrealistic, but looking back, I was talking like I could just build my own handyman business easy, like it was basically already going to work out because I knew I could do it.

I remember telling people, kind of strongly too, that I didn’t need that building, that they made a big mistake letting me go, and I was going to show them. Like, I had this feeling that I was more capable than people had given me credit for, and that once I got started, everybody would see it. I wasn’t just hoping it might work — I was talking like it was obvious, like there was no way I wouldn’t pull it off.

It’s a little embarrassing saying it now, because I was really full of that feeling then. I felt like, “I can do this, I can prove them all wrong,” and I was saying it to people like I had everything figured out already.
During that charged-up period, did you have any experiences where you heard or saw things that other people couldn’t, or believed something others said wasn’t true?

No, I don’t think so. Not like hearing voices or seeing things that weren’t there, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I was really worked up and I had a lot of confidence, probably too much, and I was convinced I could make things happen. But I don’t remember anything like seeing something other people didn’t see, or hearing someone talking when nobody was there.

And as far as believing something that wasn’t true… I don’t know. I believed in my plans way too strongly, maybe, and other people probably thought I was getting ahead of myself. But it wasn’t like I thought people were sending me messages or anything like that. It was more just me being sure of myself and pushing hard with it.
Did that charged-up, high-energy period last 4 days or more in a row?

Yeah… it was more than four days. It wasn’t just like one good day where I got wound up and then came back down.

That whole scary swing, from right after I got fired and felt driven, like I had to prove something and get moving, to then ending up as low as I’ve been feeling… that’s been going on about a month altogether. The charged-up part was definitely several days in a row, not just a short burst. I kind of lost track of the exact days because it all blurred together, but it wasn’t a weekend or anything like that. It stretched on.

target_item.manifestation: For a while I could not sit still and kept cleaning tools, moving boxes around, and planning jobs like I had a motor running in me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the charged-up period, there was an abnormal increase in activities or projects, which directly matches increased activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I was doing way more than I normally do. It was like I couldn’t sit still at all, like if I sat down for even a minute my body would start buzzing and I’d think, no, I need to get up, I need to do something.

I kept going out and cleaning my tools, even stuff that didn’t really need cleaning. doctor.question: During that charged-up period, were you talking a lot more than usual?

patient.answer:
Yeah… I guess I was. I didn’t really notice it at first, because in my head it felt like I was just explaining what needed to happen, you know? Like I had all these thoughts lined up and I had to get them out before I lost them.

I was going on and on about prices, and making flyers, and what to say to tenants, and how much things should cost, and how I was going to handle everything. I remember her trying to ask me something, and I’d just keep talking over her, not even meaning to be rude exactly, but I couldn’t stop long enough to let her catch up.

It was like my mouth was trying to keep up with my head, and there was too much coming at once.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included risky or impulsive behavior, which helps distinguish hypomania/bipolar II from a stress reaction or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, did you do anything unusually risky or impulsive for you?

target_item.reason: The question asks about unusually risky or impulsive behavior during the charged-up period, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item covering risky or impulsive activities.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that one. I mean, “risky” can mean different things, right? Like, if you mean did I go out and do something crazy dangerous on purpose, I don’t know that I’d say it that way.

During that time I was definitely acting faster than I normally would, like making decisions before really thinking them through all the way. But when you ask if it was unusually risky or impulsive, I kind of have to stop and think, because in the moment it didn’t feel risky to me. It felt like I was just doing what needed to be done, like I was finally moving instead of sitting around.

Other people might’ve seen it as me being impulsive, I guess, because I wasn’t exactly pausing and weighing things out. But I don’t have one clear thing in my head where I can say, yes, that was definitely some big risky thing. It was more like everything felt urgent, and I’d just jump into stuff without the usual hesitation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/charged period lasted at least 4 days continuously, which best distinguishes a hypomanic episode from a brief stress reaction and supports bipolar II disorder over depressive/anxiety diagnoses.
doctor.question: About how many days in a row did that charged-up period last?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The scary swing from feeling driven after I was fired to being this low has been going on for about a month.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the charged-up period lasted, which directly concerns the overall duration information in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
It’s kind of hard to pin down exactly to the day, because it didn’t feel like it started and stopped clean, like flipping a switch. But if I’m being honest, that whole scary swing — from when I got fired and then started feeling all driven and wound up, to now being this low — it’s been about a month altogether.

The charged-up part was in there first, after I got fired, and then it… shifted. But the whole thing, the whole run of it where I haven’t felt like myself, has been around a month.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable period lasted at least 4 days, which would distinguish hypomania from a shorter stress reaction and help separate bipolar II disorder from depressive and anxiety-related diagnoses.
doctor.question: Did that charged-up period last at least 4 days in a row?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The scary swing from feeling driven after I was fired to being this low has been going on for about a month.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the charged-up period lasted, specifically whether it lasted at least 4 days in a row, so the duration item is most directly relevant.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to separate it out day by day. It wasn’t like I woke up one morning and could say, okay, this is day one, and then it ended cleanly.

What I can say is that the whole scary swing — from after I got fired, when I started feeling really driven and wound up, to where I am now feeling low — has been going on for about a month. The charged-up part was at the beginning of that. I just don’t know exactly how many days to count for that piece by itself.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the charged-up period caused clear impairment or hospitalization, which helps distinguish hypomania from mania and narrows the diagnosis toward bipolar II vs other causes.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, did it cause serious problems in your life or lead to you being hospitalized?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since this got bad, I have needed my relatives to help with money, rides, and paperwork, and I am not keeping up with basic errands the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the charged-up period caused serious life problems or required hospitalization, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I didn’t go to the hospital, no. But serious problems… yeah, I mean, it’s been serious in the sense that I’m not functioning like I normally would.

Since it got bad, I’ve had to lean on my relatives for stuff I used to handle myself. Like money things, getting rides places, dealing with paperwork — forms and calls and things like that. I’ll look at something basic that needs to be done and it just doesn’t get done, or I need somebody to sit with me or take me there or remind me what I’m supposed to do.

And errands too. I’m not keeping up with regular errands the way I used to. It’s embarrassing to say, because I’m grown and I don’t like needing that much help, but right now I kind of do. So not hospitalized, but it has definitely messed up my life and made me depend on family more than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included racing thoughts, which would further support a hypomanic episode over unipolar depression or anxiety.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, did your thoughts feel like they were racing?

target_item.name: Racing_Thoughts
target_item.manifestation: My head was full of ideas all at once, one job turning into another plan, and I could not slow it down even when I tried.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether, during the charged-up period, the patient's thoughts felt like they were racing.

patient.answer:
Yes. That was actually one of the things that scared me, because it wasn’t just like normal thinking or being busy in my head. It felt like my head was packed full of ideas all at once, like one thing would pop up and before I even finished thinking about it, it turned into another plan, and then that would turn into something else.

Like I’d think about one job, or getting work, or fixing one problem, and then suddenly I’d be making this whole other plan in my mind, and then another one after that. It just kept going. I’d try to slow it down, like tell myself, “Okay, just focus on one thing,” but I couldn’t really hold it still. My thoughts kept jumping ahead of me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included increased goal-directed activity, a core hypomanic symptom that would help distinguish bipolar II disorder from unipolar depression or anxiety-related conditions.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, were you more goal-directed than usual?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I started calling old tenants, making lists, pricing tools, and trying to line up handyman work all day, way more than I ever did before.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the charged-up period involved being more goal-directed than usual, which directly matches increased goal-directed activity.

patient.answer:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, way more than normal for me. I wasn’t just thinking, “I should find some work,” I was kind of acting like I had to build this whole thing right then.

I started calling old tenants I knew, people from before, asking if they needed repairs or knew anybody who did. Then I was making lists — like long lists — of what I could fix, what tools I’d need, what I already had, what I’d have to buy. I was pricing tools, looking at costs, trying to figure out how to line up handyman work, and I’d be doing that all day.

It felt like I couldn’t just leave it alone. Normally I might make one phone call or write down a couple things and then come back to it later, but during that time I was pushing and pushing, like every minute had to be used to get something started. It was a lot more than I’d ever done before.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the charged-up period included grandiosity, which would strengthen bipolar II disorder over a stress-related or unipolar depressive condition.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, did you feel more powerful, special, or capable than usual?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I was telling people I could build my own handyman business easy and show that building they made a big mistake letting me go.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the charged-up period, the patient felt unusually powerful, special, or capable, which directly matches inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, I did. At the time it didn’t feel like I was being unrealistic, but looking back, I was talking like I could just build my own handyman business easy, like it was basically already going to work out because I knew I could do it.

I remember telling people, kind of strongly too, that I didn’t need that building, that they made a big mistake letting me go, and I was going to show them. Like, I had this feeling that I was more capable than people had given me credit for, and that once I got started, everybody would see it. I wasn’t just hoping it might work — I was talking like it was obvious, like there was no way I wouldn’t pull it off.

It’s a little embarrassing saying it now, because I was really full of that feeling then. I felt like, “I can do this, I can prove them all wrong,” and I was saying it to people like I had everything figured out already.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated period included psychotic features, which would distinguish bipolar I manic episode from bipolar II hypomania and major depressive presentations.
doctor.question: During that charged-up period, did you have any experiences where you heard or saw things that other people couldn’t, or believed something others said wasn’t true?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hallucinations or delusional beliefs during the charged-up period, but the provided symptom profile does not include psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think so. Not like hearing voices or seeing things that weren’t there, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I was really worked up and I had a lot of confidence, probably too much, and I was convinced I could make things happen. But I don’t remember anything like seeing something other people didn’t see, or hearing someone talking when nobody was there.

And as far as believing something that wasn’t true… I don’t know. I believed in my plans way too strongly, maybe, and other people probably thought I was getting ahead of myself. But it wasn’t like I thought people were sending me messages or anything like that. It was more just me being sure of myself and pushing hard with it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/charged-up period met the minimum duration for a hypomanic episode, which best distinguishes bipolar II disorder from depressive/anxiety or stress-related conditions.
doctor.question: Did that charged-up, high-energy period last 4 days or more in a row?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: The scary swing from feeling driven after I was fired to being this low has been going on for about a month.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the charged-up, high-energy period lasted, which is directly about duration.

patient.answer:
Yeah… it was more than four days. It wasn’t just like one good day where I got wound up and then came back down.

That whole scary swing, from right after I got fired and felt driven, like I had to prove something and get moving, to then ending up as low as I’ve been feeling… that’s been going on about a month altogether. The charged-up part was definitely several days in a row, not just a short burst. I kind of lost track of the exact days because it all blurred together, but it wasn’t a weekend or anything like that. It stretched on.

inference.note: Current history supports a major depressive episode plus a distinct hypomanic episode lasting >4 days with decreased need for sleep, increased talkativeness, racing thoughts, increased goal-directed activity, elevated/irritable mood and inflated confidence, without psychosis or hospitalization. This narrows away F32.A, F41.9, F50.9, and F54 as primary diagnoses.
